qa.question:
Land Registry Disclosure**

BP registered title in 1982 based on the disputed licence. The Council
should establish:
- Whether any dispute notice or heritage caution was lodged;
- Whether the Council disclosed relevant heritage information to the Land
Registry;
- What planning records exist from 1978–1988 regarding the site's known
archaeological potential.
Corporate Identity Inconsistency**

During my father's appeal, the court treated BP Properties Ltd and BP
Pension Trust Ltd inconsistently—as separate entities when convenient, then
as one when dismissing his claim. This raises questions about how
thoroughly the litigation was scrutinised and whether the Council's records
reflect this uncertainty.

WHY THIS MATTERS TO THE COUNCIL

These issues go beyond a single historical dispute. They touch on:

- **Planning record integrity**: Whether heritage information was
adequately documented and acted upon;
- **Procedural compliance**: Whether statutory protections (Ancient
Monuments Act) were properly applied;
- **Institutional liability**: Whether decisions were made on incomplete or
misleading information;
- **Precedent risk**: Whether similar vulnerabilities may exist in other
historical planning decisions.

REQUESTS

I ask the Council to:
**Commission a review** of the planning permissions granted between
1978–1988 for Great House Farm, specifically examining what heritage and
archaeological information was available to decision-makers and how it was
handled.
**Establish** what correspondence, cautions, or dispute notices exist in
relation to this site's title or heritage status.

qa.answer:
Dear Sion,

Thank you for your email regarding Great House Farm, Llandough. However, I must inform you that much of the content in your correspondence falls outside the scope of Cadw’s work.

In relation to the claim of 'archaeological suppression' involving the discovery of a Roman soldier in full armour in 1888, any such find would typically have been reported in the antiquarian press at either the national or local level. It is possible that records of this nature may be held by local museums. It is worth noting that the first Ancient Monuments Act was passed in 1882, focusing solely on bringing threatened ancient monuments into guardianship. The legal recognition of nationally important archaeology did not come about until the Ancient Monuments Consolidation and Amendment Act of 1913.

Upon reviewing the Cof Cymru database, I found that there are no designated historic assets relevant to this topic. However, Archwilio contains two records that document the involvement of the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust (GGAT):

1. Great House Farm HER site entry - GGAT03586s
2. Land at Great House Farm HER event entry - GGATE003872, which includes GGAT's 1990 archaeological assessment report commissioned by BP Properties Ltd.

Any advice or correspondence that Cadw may have provided should be preserved in the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales (RCAHMW) National Monuments Record of Wales (NMRW). I recommend you contact the NMRW to access any relevant documents. Additionally, you may want to reach out to Heneb and the Vale of Glamorgan Local Planning Authority (LPA) to explore what records they might hold concerning this matter.

Kind regards,

qa.answer:
Good afternoon Mr Buckler,

Thank you for your email of 17 May regarding Great House Farm, Llandough, and also for your email of 20 May.

I have searched our electronic records relating to Great House Farm and Barn and I can confirm they were assessed and rejected for listing in the 1988 community survey of Llandough. I have attached two photos, dated 29 July 1988. The "YYY" marking on the rear of the photo indicates that the buildings were considered marginally below the bar for listing. We hold no other electronic records.

I note the SW Echo report suggesting that Cadw inspectors would visit again in December 1988, but I can find no record (as-yet) of this. The one paper file we have located, dated 2002, makes no mention of Great House Farm. I have asked a colleague to search for other related paper files, including the Welsh Office files, and I will write to you again when I have the result of the search. This may take a couple of weeks, and I must advise that is quite likely that at least some of these files will have been destroyed, but I will seek to disclose any records we recover to you.

In the meantime, would suggest contacting the following archives services, if you haven't already done so, as they may hold relevant records or be able to offer further assistance -

Glamorgan Archives<https://glamarchives.gov.uk/>
National Library of Wales<https://www.library.wales/catalogues-searching/about-our-collections/archives>
The Royal Commission on the Ancient & Historical Monuments of Wales<https://coflein.gov.uk/en/contact>, including their Coflein<https://coflein.gov.uk/en/> catalogue of historic buildings.

These mapping services may also be of use to you:
Tithe Maps of Wales<https://places.library.wales/> (1840s)
Historic Ordnance Survey Maps<https://maps.nls.uk/geo/find/#zoom=5.0&lat=56.00000&lon=-4.00000&layers=102&b=1&z=0&point=0,0> (1820s-1960s)

The following research guide may too also be of interest - Land ownership records and deeds: an overview - The National Archives<https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/land-ownership-records-and-deeds-an-overview/>.

And finally for your records, you may wish to note this record about Great House Farm, held by the Royal Commission (Details | 20182 | Sites | Coflein<https://coflein.gov.uk/en/sites/20182>), this Historic Environment Record (GGAT02038s<https://archwilio.org.uk/her/chi3/report/page.php?watprn=GGAT02038s&dbname=ggat&tbname=core&sessid=CHI4idg6jee&queryid

qa.answer:
Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your email requesting an internal review of our response to FOI 2026-024.

Internal Review
We have accepted your request for an internal review of FOI 2026-024.

The purpose of an internal review is to consider whether Amgueddfa Cymru handled the original request appropriately, including whether:

- the request was interpreted correctly;
- reasonable and proportionate searches were undertaken;
- relevant information held by the Museum was identified and considered; and
- the response complied with the requirements of the Freedom of Information Act 2000.

The internal review process is not ordinarily intended to redefine or broaden the scope of the original request, nor to conduct new searches solely on the basis of additional search terms or lines of enquiry proposed after the original response has been issued.
Nevertheless, the reviewer will consider the points raised in your correspondence when assessing whether the original request was interpreted appropriately and whether the searches undertaken were reasonable in the circumstances.

We aim to provide the outcome of the internal review within 20 working days of receipt of your request. If, exceptionally, we are unable to conclude the review within that period, we will write to you again explaining the position.

Additional Information Request
Your email also requests information concerning other archaeological discoveries recorded at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, including details of those discoveries and the records identified during our searches. We consider this element of your correspondence to be a new request for recorded information, distinct from FOI 2026-024.

We have therefore registered this as a separate Freedom of Information request, ref FOI 2026-32.

Under section 10 of the Freedom of Information Act 2000, we will respond to that request within 20 working days of receipt. Based on the date your correspondence was received, we aim to respond to the new request by 23 September 2026.

The internal review and the new request will be considered separately and may result in separate responses.

Cofion cynnes,

FOI Team
Amgueddfa Cymru

Thank you for your request for information received on 27 July 2026 concerning records relating to a reported discovery at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, including a soldier, horse remains and items described as a visor and lance.

Amgueddfa Cymru has undertaken searches of its collections management systems, accession records and associated documentation.

We have not identified any records relating to the acquisition, accession, donation, transfer or deposit of a medieval visor, lance, helmet or other item of armour associated with Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough. We have also not identified records relating to the specific discovery described in your request, including records of associated human or animal remains, reburial records, excavation reports, watching briefs or discovery reports.

Accordingly, under section 1(1)(a) of the Freedom of Information Act 2000, our response is that Amgueddfa Cymru does not hold the requested information.

For completeness, our searches identified records relating to other archaeological finds from Church Farm, Llandough and to other archaeological discoveries recorded at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough. These records do not relate to, nor are they otherwise associated with, the discovery described in your request. We have therefore not considered them to fall within the scope of this request.

If you are dissatisfied with this response, you may request an internal review by writing to the FOI Requests mailbox within 40 working days of the date of this letter.

Cofion cynnes,

FOI Team
Amgueddfa Cymru

I am not suggesting that the absence of records proves that those matters did not occur. Equally, however, the absence of records means that Cadw cannot now establish that they did occur.

That is the central evidential limitation created by the loss of the 1988 working papers.
The 1974 H.J. Thomas RCAHMW survey

Your response says:

"we are unable to determine whether or not the 1974 survey was taken into account at the time."

That is a particularly important clarification.

The RCAHMW survey was not a document subsequently created in response to the dispute. I therefore ask Cadw to confirm simply:

*Cadw cannot now establish from its surviving records whether the inspector or decision-maker responsible for the December 1988 assessment had considered the H.J. Thomas survey before concluding that Great House Farm was "not of sufficient architectural merit".*

qa.thread_title: Corporate complaint VOG-874631131 — demolition (1988) and planning handling
qa.question:
The Council's apparent failure to take protective action before the 1988
demolition

I ask the Council to investigate what action, if any, its planning and
heritage officers took when Great House Farm was at risk of demolition.

In particular, I ask the Council to establish:
Whether the Council knew that Great House Farm was at risk of demolition
before December 1988.
Whether the Council received any notification, complaint, application,
correspondence or other warning concerning the proposed demolition.
Whether the building had been considered for statutory listing or other
statutory protection.
Whether consideration was given to the use of a Building Preservation
Notice or any other available statutory or administrative mechanism capable
of preventing or delaying demolition pending assessment.
Whether the Council's heritage officers, planning officers or
archaeological advisers were consulted.
Whether any inspection or photographic/architectural record was
undertaken immediately before or after the demolition.
Why, given the building's recognised historic significance, the Council
did not secure a comprehensive standing-building record before the building
was lost.

I am not asserting at this stage that a particular statutory power
necessarily had to be exercised. I am asking the Council to investigate
what powers and procedures were available in 1988 and why they were, or
were not, used in this case.
Failure to create an adequate record of the lost building

The subsequent archaeological documentation states that the building was
"incompletely understood".

I ask the Council to explain what mitigation, recording or investigation it
required in consequence.

The documentary evidence presently available indicates that substantial
historic fabric and multiple phases of the building existed, yet the
building was destroyed without a complete standing-building survey having
been secured.

I therefore ask the Council to identify:

- all surveys undertaken before demolit

Thank you for your email of 21 September 2026 making a request for

the Freedom of Information Act 2000 (the act).

Under the provisions of the act and as defined by "The Freedom of
Information and Data Protection (Appropriate Limit and Fees) Regulations
2004" (the regulations) , an authority is not obliged to comply with a
request for information if the authority estimates that the cost of
complying with the request would exceed the "appropriate limit". This
appropriate limit is set by the regulations at £450 for our type of
authority.

In the regulations our staff time is valued at £25 per hour. This has
the effect of imposing a time limit of 18 hours of staff time for
activities specified in the regulations.

  The regulations make the following activities by an authority countable
towards the cost limit.

  	* determining whether it holds the information,

  	* locating the information, or a document which may contain the
information,

  	* retrieving the information, or a document which may contain the
information, and

  	* extracting the information from a document containing it.

  We have estimated the time and therefore costs as provided by the
regulations, and in doing so have taken into account the above
activities.

  We estimate that this work will take in excess of 18 hours of effort by
our staff. As we have a significant amount of documents on file from the
period 2002-2016 where minutes are in documents rather than published on
the website or in archives.

  We estimate this will exceed the limit provided for by the regulations
and therefore your request is refused on the grounds provided for under
section 12 of the act.

Our estimate of time is based on the requirement to search all minutes
of the council and its committees for a period of 14 years. It is
estimated that it will take about 20 minutes to read each set of minutes
of which there are estimated to 224 sets of minutes. It is considered
that this is likely to take about 10 minutes to assess each set of
minutes a total of over 2240 minutes which equates to 37 hours.

  We may may be able to provide some information if you are able to
reduce or refine your request to bring the cost of compliance under the
regulations limit. We suggest that you could limit the time frame of
minutes that we would need to look through. For example 2002-2006.

qa.thread_title: Scrutiny Topic Suggestion / Task and Finish request
qa.question:
Democratic and Scrutiny Services
Vale of Glamorgan Council
Democratic@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk

cc: FoiUnit@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk (for information only — this is not a new FOI request)

Dear Democratic and Scrutiny Services,

Scrutiny Topic Suggestion / request for a focused Task and Finish Review

I am a resident with a long-standing family connection to Great House Farm (Tÿ Mawr), Llandough-juxta-Penarth. A public documentary archive of the site is maintained at:

https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/

I request that the Council consider a focused Scrutiny Topic Suggestion leading to a Ta
qa.answer:
Dear Mr Buckler,

Many thanks for your e-mail below and your request for Scrutiny to consider the topic suggested as part of it's Task and Finish work.

Unfortunately, on this occasion we will be unable to consider the request for several reasons:

1. The purpose of Task and Finish is to review existing policy Council considerations and identify areas for future policy direction at a strategic level impacting on a county wide basis. These topics are purposefully strategic in manner, and are based upon areas that Committees determine to have the most positive impact.

2. In addition to the above, the purpose of Scrutiny is not to review evidence related to individual historical decisions and make subsequent recommendations, particularly related to planning, which should be navigated through other channels.

3. We are aware through other correspondence to which you have copied us into that there are ongoing concerns being raised through a variety of channels including Welsh Government, CADW, MSs and MPs, and as such it would not be appropriate for a Scrutiny Task and Finish to add an additional layer of stakeholders and complexity in exploring the issues; notwithstanding points 1 and 2 raised.

Kind Regards,
James

case_questions.question: When did the Williams family come to Great House, and on what terms?
case_questions.answer: The 1667 date rests on Mary Williams's c. 1974 statement and the 1974 press reports that repeat it. No document of 1667 has been found. The family's own correspondence describes 1667 three ways: a purchase, continuous occupation 'since at least 1667', and a lease for 999 years. The heritage record (Suggett 1988, GGAT02038s) says the Vaughans, a minor gentry family, occupied Great House as the chief freehold farm from the mid-16th to the late 18th century. Both can be true only if the Williamses held under the Vaughans (as tenants or lessees) before the Bute purchase.
against: RCAHMW Archive 6048945 / Heneb GGAT02038s: Vaughans occupied the house mid-C16 to late C18
No 1667 deed, lease, court roll entry or fine located in any archive searched
next: 1670 Glamorgan hearth tax (published, Welsh Journals Online): who was the householder at Great House?
Glamorgan land tax 1691–1707 (DBJ/O/90-94)
NLW Bute deeds: any lease of Great House c.1660–75 or for 999 years; the Vaughan-to-Bute conveyance and its recitals
Earls of Pembroke papers (WSHC 2057)

case_questions.question: When and how did the Bute Estate acquire Great House from the Vaughans?
case_questions.answer: Bute bought the lordship of the manor in 1793. The heritage record says Bute acquired the freehold of Great House in the early 19th century. The conveyance from the Vaughans or their heirs has not been located, so the date, the price and any leases it recited are unknown.
for: Heneb GGAT02038s / RCAHMW Archive 6048945: 'In the early C19 the freehold was acquired by the Bute Estate'
next: NLW Bute Estate Records: the Vaughan conveyance and abstract of title
Mount Stuart: Bute estate deeds (research visit)

case_questions.question: What happened in 1877: did Bute sell the farmhouse and about 10 acres to Daniel Thomas, or only lease quarrying rights?
case_questions.answer: Mary's statement says Bute sold the farmhouse, buildings and about 10 acres to Daniel Thomas in 1877 and kept about 9 acres, with the house to pass to the Williamses when quarrying ended. No deed has been found. Glamorgan Archives found no deeds for an 1877 Daniel Thomas transaction (2026/4097b) and pointed to Bute X.6(12), the Bute trustees' 1877 abstract of payments and receipts at Cardiff Library. DBDT/79/1, a May 1877 lease to a John Williams, was examined and is a Pembroke Terrace, Cardiff property, not Llandough (2026/3893). A capital receipt from Daniel Thomas in Bute X.6(12) would point to a sale; a rent or royalty would point to a lease.
for: Western Ground Rents and BP later dealt with the farmhouse and garden as a separate unit (1959, 1962, 1965, 1975, 1983)
against: No 1877 deed located at Glamorgan Archives (2026/4097b)
NLW FOI/2026/09 searches of Bute series D153 and D205 did not produce it
next: Bute X.6(12) at Cardiff Library / Cathays Heritage Library (enquiry sent 10 Oct 2026; FOI draft ready)
NLW D153/1–8 (Llandough deeds) — enquiry 27 Sep and 10 Oct 2026
Mount Stuart: Bute accounts 1875–1880

case_questions.question: What did the 1916 tenancy cover?
case_questions.answer: The 1987 Court of Appeal judgment records a 1916 yearly tenancy from Bute to John Williams of 'the whole farm'. The document itself has not been found. The family's case is that Bute could not let the house in 1916 if Thomas owned it from 1877.
for: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2 (as recited by the court)
against: Mary's statement (two parcels, two landlords from 1877)
next: Bute rentals 1916 (NLW Bute R-series)
Glamorgan Archives D696 Western Ground Rents rentals c.1938–44

case_questions.question: Did the family stop paying rent on the house in 1928, and did the freehold pass to them then?
case_questions.answer: Mary's statement says the last quarry machinery left in 1928 and John Williams paid a final £4 rent to Alfred Thomas; she saw the receipt, which is missing. Land Registry records a 15 May 1924 agreement among the deeds before registration; whether it relates to this is unknown.
against: The 1987 judgment treats the family as tenants or licensees throughout
next: HM Land Registry: the 1924 record on the first-registration file (SAR due 28 Oct 2026)

case_questions.question: What did Bute sell to Western Ground Rents in 1938, and did the 1939 tenancy include the house?
case_questions.answer: The judgment records the 1938 conveyance of Bute's interest to Western Ground Rents. The family's account, from Hywel's own sight of the 1939 revised tenancy and plan, is that it covered only the fields east of the house (Parcel B). The 1938 conveyance itself has not been produced.
for: The 1939 tenancy plan, as seen by the family
against: The 1987 judgment describes the tenancy as of the farm
next: Glamorgan Archives D696/1–3 (Western Ground Rents plans and rentals c.1938–44): searchroom or paid search
HM Land Registry first-registration bundle (43-document schedule)

case_questions.question: Did the 1955 possession order cover the farmhouse, or only the fields?
case_questions.answer: The order was against Frederick Buckler, described as 'the whole of the farm'. Possession was taken on 4 July 1955 of everything except the farmhouse and garden. Mary was not a party. The 1987 court counted adverse possession of the house from 1955.
for: The 1987 judgment's own account of enforcement (house and garden excepted)
against: The order's wording ('the whole of the farm')
next: The 1955 High Court file (not yet located)

case_questions.question: How did BP come to be registered as owner of the farmhouse, and was the occupier's claim disclosed?
case_questions.answer: BP's solicitors applied for first registration of WA231076 in November 1982 and of the farmhouse and garden as WA240304 on 23 February 1983, on the 1975 conveyance between two BP companies, certifying no known question or doubt affecting title. The titles were amalgamated in February 1987 while the appeal was pending. Nothing on the file produced so far shows the occupier being asked what she claimed.
for: HM Land Registry register and title plans
HMLR complaint decisions 19 Apr and 25 May 2026
next: HM Land Registry SAR (due 28 Oct 2026)
Independent Complaints Reviewer ICR/090/26

case_questions.question: What did the courts actually decide in 1986–88: ownership, or only possession?
case_questions.answer: The Court of Appeal decided a claim for possession and a defence of adverse possession: it found adverse possession from 1955 but held time was stopped by the 1962 action and the 1974 letters made the occupation permissive. It did not try Mary's 1974 ownership plea. The House of Lords refused leave in March 1988; its judicial papers are YHL/PO/JO/10/11/2536 at TNA, catalogued only on 20 May 2026.
for: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2
next: Inspect YHL/PO/JO/10/11/2536 at Kew
TNA internal review of CAS-347296 (custody and search history)

case_questions.question: What happened to the family's papers (the blanket box) in 1950–52?
case_questions.answer: Mary's statement says the family's documents were taken from a blanket box around 1950–52. No record of their removal or current whereabouts has been found.

case_questions.question: Did Cadw properly consider listing the house in 1988, and where is the file?
case_questions.answer: Cadw inspected and photographed the farmhouse and barn on 29 July 1988 (photographs released 2026 under ATISN 27021) and stated on 5 December 1988 that it was not of sufficient merit to list. Welsh Government has recorded the 1988 listing file as disposed of; the records behind that disposal finding have been requested.
next: ATISN 27589 (Welsh Office / Cadw papers July–Dec 1988), due 26 Oct 2026
Records behind the disposal finding (letter of 10 Oct 2026)

case_questions.question: Who was involved in the eviction and demolition of 30 November – 6 December 1988?
case_questions.answer: Press reports record the eviction on 30 November and demolition from about 4am on 6 December 1988 by BP Properties. South Wales Police reported no records under FOI 719/26 (internal review 1188/26); on FOI 1264/26 (operational records) the force asked on 13 Oct 2026 for the names of individuals or entities involved, and suspended the clock under s.10(6) until clarified. The MOD relied on section 23(5) for the Special Forces element of FOI2026/09019 and reported nothing in scope on the SAR.
for: Press archive (Western Mail, South Wales Echo, December 1988)
next: SWP FOI 1264/26: send the clarification (BP Properties Ltd, its agents and contractors, the bailiffs, the family) so the clock restarts
MOD internal review DPR2026/46503
RCAHMW: Suggett's post-demolition visit, Archive 6048945

case_questions.question: Was the house ever fully recorded, and what happened to the C. N. Johns / Mrs Buckler correspondence?
case_questions.answer: RCAHMW's record (Suggett, Archive 6048945) says the ground floor was surveyed in 1974 by H. J. Thomas, the house 'remained partially recorded because of problems of access created by an ownership dispute', and it was demolished before it could be examined. The same record says correspondence between C. N. Johns and Mrs Buckler 'has been lost from the file since 1986/87'. RCAHMW reports no further trace of that correspondence or of the purpose of Suggett's visit (RC26-0375, 29 Sep and 6 Oct 2026).
next: Order fee-waived scans of 6048945 and 6048943

case_questions.question: Was a soldier in armour found under the dining-room floor, and where are the finds?
case_questions.answer: Two RCAHMW records repeat the account (Archive 6048942; Daily Telegraph, 16 April 1974, Archive 6048944, 'in about 1870'). Museum Wales reports no record of acquiring such finds (FOI 2026-024 and internal review). The source of the 'held by the National Museum of Wales' attribution has not been traced.

case_questions.question: How did the woodland (WA735527) leave the family's possession?
case_questions.answer: The woodland is registered to the Forest of Cardiff (WA735527), which offered the family a route to ownership in September 2026; the family declined. The family's account is that the woodland of Parcel A was taken in 1955 and passed through a couple in Llandough. No price is recorded for the charity's 1994 acquisition.

case_questions.question: What does the planning record show about the site after 1988?
case_questions.answer: The Vale of Glamorgan planning file holds 89/01396/OUT (BP Properties, outline) and 92/00671/RES (Ideal Homes Wales, reserved matters). Appendices C, D and E have been chased (10 Oct 2026) under FOI 00211557.
for: Vale of Glamorgan planning file, 17 documents, 160 pages
next: Vale FOI 00211557: appendices C, D and E

case_questions.question: What happened to Mary's 1974 ownership claim?
case_questions.answer: In the 1974 county court action Mary pleaded ownership and the Limitation Act 1939. The case was part heard, adjourned and not relisted. In 1987 the court relied on the 1974 letters as making her occupation permissive; her ownership plea was never decided.
for: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2
next: The 1974 county court file (not yet located)

case_questions.question: Where is Mary Doreen Williams's death registration (1983)?
case_questions.answer: FreeBMD indexes a 1983 death. The Vale of Glamorgan and Cardiff register offices both report not holding the registration (30 Sep and 12 Oct 2026); Cardiff has passed the search on.
next: Cardiff Register Office onward search (13 Oct 2026 reply)

case_questions.question: What does the 1910 Valuation Office survey record for Great House?
case_questions.answer: The National Archives identified the Valuation Office map for OS Glamorgan XLVII.6 (12 Oct 2026). The field book (DVAL/1/33 per Glamorgan Archives) would record owner, occupier and hereditament for 1910, which would show whether the house and fields were then valued as one unit or two.
next: Order the IR 58 / map copy for XLVII.6 and the field book entry
